name: Safflower-petal lipstick

lead:
Beni is a lip color made from the red pigment of safflower petals. Applied in thin layers with a brush it builds from a soft stain to a deep crimson with a green sheen, used to define and color the lips.
It was a luxury cosmetic in Japan well before the Edo period and is still made by a few firms. A single small pot takes around 1,000 blossoms.

paras: Traditionally it is dried in a porcelain pot or on a dish, wetted and painted onto the lips or eyelids in layers; more layers give a deeper, greener finish. Modern versions come as sticks and pots.
As a plant-derived pigment it is generally treated like any cosmetic; no particular hazards are described, though sensitivity to plant materials can occur.

web.title: The Shade That Lasted 200 Years: Inside Isehan's Japanese Beauty Legacy

angle.text: Beni colors the lips directly, from a faint blush to a jewel-like crimson depending on layers, and is also used on the eyelids.[2]

lead: Beni is a traditional Japanese cosmetic made from the red pigment of safflower petals, used mainly on the lips to give color and, when layered, an iridescent green sheen.[1] It improves looks by tinting and defining the mouth and, according to makers, can also be used on the eyelids.[1]

The red coloring in safflower is carthamin; the petals also contain yellow dyes.[2] Safflower dye was costly and sometimes diluted.[2] Isehan, founded in 1825 in Edo, still makes Komachi-beni by hand.[1]

paras: The red pigment carthamin, also called Carthamus Red, is one red and two yellow dyes found in the petals.[2] Beni looks crimson in direct light and shows a greenish shimmer when tilted.[1] About 1,000 blossoms go into one small pot.[1]

Isehan's maker says beni signalled sophistication among upper-class women and was believed to aid circulation and protect against evil spirits.[1] Safflower dye itself has been used since antiquity, including in Egyptian textiles.[2]

timeline.event: Isehan begins making beni in Edo.[1]
